Young platings of Rainbow-lipped pearl oyster (Pteria sterna) originate from fertilised eggs measuring approximately 40 micrometres in diameter. The resulting planktonic veliger larvae undergo a period of endogenous feeding before transitioning to exogenous feeding on phytoplankton. Following larval metamorphosis and settlement, the newly attached spat exhibit a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0000000335 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0000000335 grams], a minuscule mass that reflects the energetic constraints of the lecithotrophic yolk-sac stage. These initial post-metamorphic juveniles, known as spat, then commence a rapid growth phase within the sheltered bays of the eastern Pacific. The protracted developmental trajectory from a free-swimming trochophore to a benthic juvenile is highly dependent on local sea surface temperatures, which modulate metabolic rates and food assimilation efficiency. Under optimal thermal regimes juveniles can achieve substantial size increases within their first year, although significant variation is observed across different microhabitats and latitudes within the species' range.

Measurements of somatic growth in wild populations of Pteria sterna indicate that the total length at which puberty is attained is 5.95 centimetres [Lp = 5.95 centimetres]. This morphometric benchmark corresponds to the onset of gametogenesis and the first visible differentiation of gonadal tissue. Individuals at this shell length redirect substantial metabolic resources toward reproductive tissue synthesis, a trade-off that becomes energetically demanding. The ultimate total length for adults in this species has been recorded at 9.5 centimetres [Li = 9.5 centimetres], based on extensive surveys of shell dimensions across multiple cohorts. Reaching this asymptotic size requires several years of sustained growth and is accompanied by a marked deceleration in somatic expansion as energy is increasingly channelled into gamete production and maintenance of existing tissues. The disparity between length at puberty and ultimate length underscores a life-history strategy in which reproduction commences well before maximum body size is achieved, a common pattern among iteroparous bivalves.

Under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable temperature of 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) was determined to be 30% [GSI = 30%]. This substantial allocation to gamete production is characteristic of bivalves that release large numbers of eggs and sperm into the water column for external fertilisation, a strategy that relies on high fecundity to offset the stochastic mortality of planktonic larvae. The flesh wet weight of reproductively active adults averages 119 grams [Wwi = 119 grams], providing the somatic infrastructure necessary to support such elevated gonadal output. These values were derived from dissections conducted during the austral summer spawning peak when energetic demands on the organism are greatest.

Longevity records for the Rainbow-lipped pearl oyster have been established through mark-recapture studies and shell growth increment analysis. At the same thermal regime of 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C], the maximum lifespan has been determined to be approximately 1825 days [am = approximately 1825 days], equivalent to about five years of sustained biological activity. This relatively modest lifespan for a marine bivalve reflects the high metabolic costs associated with living in warm, productive coastal waters where predation pressure and parasitic loads also contribute to elevated mortality rates. Older individuals often exhibit extensive shell bioerosion and reduced fecundity, suggesting the onset of reproductive senescence in the final year of life. The synchrony between high water temperature, accelerated metabolic demand, and maximum longevity indicates that the species' physiological clock is tightly coupled to ambient thermal conditions, with cooler waters potentially extending the lifespan beyond the documented five-year benchmark.

The life-history strategy of Pteria sterna reveals a clear separation between the onset of reproduction and the attainment of maximum body size. Puberty occurs at a shell length of 5.95 centimetres [Lp = 5.95 centimetres], while adults can continue growing until reaching an ultimate shell length of 9.5 centimetres [Li = 9.5 centimetres]. This reproductive timing is supported by an adult flesh wet weight of 119 grams [Wwi = 119 grams], providing adequate metabolic reserves for both gametogenesis and somatic maintenance. The gonadosomatic index of 30% [GSI = 30%] was recorded at 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C]. Ultimately, the maximum lifespan of approximately 1825 days [am = approximately 1825 days] encapsulates a life cycle characterized by rapid juvenile growth and early sexual maturation, typical of tropical bivalves inhabiting warm coastal waters at a temperature of 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C].
